principles.text: Before shorting a bounce, check where the index AND the sector ETF sit relative to their declining 9 EMA: if they are still extended below it, they will likely keep bouncing into the declining 9/21 and drag your stock up with them (~70-80% of stocks follow market/sector). Short when the index/sector has already bounced back near its declining EMAs, not before.

Shorting every bounce into the declining 9 EMA has the lowest win rate of pullback-short entries — the 9 is the fastest EMA and pullbacks routinely extend to the 21 or even the 50 before rolling over.

Pullback shorts need bear-market context, not just a red week: an intact weekly uptrend making its FIRST pullback into the rising weekly 21 usually finds support and starts another leg; markets rarely slice through all the EMAs without a bounce or sideways attempt first. Shorting that is completely different from shorting a 3-month downtrend where the 50 EMA is under the 150, the declining EMAs are clustered, and breadth is broken.
Do not short immediately after a strong reversal candle — one that opened lower, recovered the whole intraday loss, and closed near the high of day and the prior day's high.

A relatively-strong stock gapping DOWN into rising daily 9/21 support while its sector ETF also opens red improves the odds of the pullback buy — you are buying support with the sector's selling already expressed (e.g. gapping down into the 9/21 on a day SOXX opens lower).

You spot the next leading theme when several names from the same group (five or six, not one or two) show up in the same day's relative-strength scans — especially if they are bouncing on a red market day.

True market leaders top BEFORE the index: QCOM topped in January 2000 while the Nasdaq ran until March. When the real leaders of the move stall, fail to make higher highs, and show relative weakness while the index grinds higher, get cautious on the whole market.

Blow-off tops print extreme dollar volume relative to market cap: QCOM traded ~1/4 of its market cap in one week at the 2000 top (SNDK ~half). Huge weekly volume expansion plus price acceleration after a long uptrend is distribution, not strength.

Watch the volatility signature, not just price: in a healthy base volatility looks like the uptrend's, but consecutive giant alternating red/green weekly candles near highs (volatility expansion) mark the late stage of a move (Motorola 2000).

True trending leaders never close below the weekly 9 EMA on the way up (QCOM never violated it through a ~600%-then-300% run; works with any fast weekly MA). Riding that line keeps you in far longer than feels comfortable — simple, powerful, and very hard to actually follow. The first weekly close below it after a long run (SNDK last week) is the warning.

Market corrections start from an EXTENSION or a FAILED BREAKOUT, almost never from a flat base or sideways range (2007, 2018 trade war, 2024 examples). If neither structure is present, it is too early to call a top.

The market won't crash in a day — a real downtrend shows multiple signs first (leader breakdowns, failed breakouts, volume/volatility expansion). Wait for the danger signs instead of front-running a top call; standing out from the crowd by top-ticking is not smart, and the market can run far beyond what you can imagine.

When neither side offers clear risk/reward — longs not yet confirmed, shorts already extended down into weekly support — trade less and smaller: 'less is more' until the market proves itself, while still probing new positions so you participate if it works.

Stocks increasingly take out the low of day and then rally back to the highs (stop-run shakeouts). If a name gets you out at LOD but falls right back into confluent support (anchored VWAP + daily 9 + clustered lower-timeframe EMAs), treat it as a re-entry candidate rather than a dead trade — but let the market/breakout buyers confirm first.

99% of trading questions have no model answer — different traders reach different, equally profitable answers. Verify claims yourself and build your own conviction; don't adopt another trader's rule without digesting it, and value the thinking process over being right.

Almost nobody does the boring off-hours study (a chart-study prompt to ~27k viewers drew 11 real replies): the repetitive, un-dopaminergic work — studying past charts, learning from mistakes when the market is closed — is itself the edge, because so few put in the time.
Study historical downtrends, not just uptrends: once for shorting skill, once for staying out of bear markets, and once for recognizing where real turning points form at the end of a decline.
History gives ideas but does not directly repeat — don't over-fit past patterns onto today's market; let current individual charts prove the thesis first.
